chunks: Ja'far ibn 'Isa wrote to him: 'May I be sacrificed for you! Neighbors of ours came to me with a document, claiming that they had made me a witness to what was in it. In the document is my name in my own handwriting, which I recognized — yet I do not remember the act of testimony. They have summoned me to testify. Shall I testify for them based on my recognition that my name is in the document, even though I do not remember the testimony — or is it not obligatory for me to give testimony for them until I remember it, regardless of whether my name is in the document in my handwriting or not?' So he wrote: 'Do not testify.'

key_terms.الشَّهَادَةَ: testimony (shahada) — the formal legal act of bearing witness before a judge or authority
key_terms.الْكِتَابِ: document/writing — a written legal instrument or contract presented as evidence
key_terms.بِخَطِّي: in my handwriting — physical script used as circumstantial evidence of prior witnessing
key_terms.مَعْرِفَتِي: my recognition — identifying something by sight or knowledge without direct memory of an act

ai.seo_question: Can a Muslim testify in court based only on recognizing their own handwriting in a document if they do not remember the act of giving testimony?
ai.summary: This hadith presents a concise but significant legal ruling on testimony (shahada) in Islamic jurisprudence. Ja'far ibn 'Isa, a companion who corresponded with the Imam, poses the question of whether recognition of one's handwriting in a document — without an actual memory of the witnessing act — is sufficient grounds to testify. The Imam's terse written reply, 'Do not testify,' reflects the Shia jurisprudential principle that valid testimony requires direct personal knowledge and certain recollection of the witnessed event, not mere inference from physical evidence. This principle protects the integrity of legal proceedings by ensuring testimony is based on genuine certainty.
